title: My Organized Home System
subtitle: Decide once, then stop deciding.
objectives: Design a storage system with a place for everything
Explain why a system must not rely on memory
Take on a fair share of household work

cards.title: A system you have to remember is not a system
cards.text: The whole term comes together here. Everything you have learned (zones, FIFO, clean-as-you-go) is the same idea: decide once, then stop deciding.

cards.title: A place for everything, decided once
cards.text: The decision is the work. After that it is just putting things back.
points: **Every object has one home.**
**The home is where it is used**, not where there is space.
**Things used daily go at hand height.**
**If you have to think about where it goes, it has no home yet.**

cards.title: Six jobs, and the skill each one builds
cards.text: Tap each job. The second line is why it is yours rather than someone else's.

question.text: Where should a daily-use item be stored?
question.explain: Storage near use is the whole rule.

cards.title: Daily, weekly, monthly
cards.text: Three loops, each with a fixed time.
points: **Daily:** dishes, surfaces, your own things away.
**Weekly:** laundry, sheets, floors, one shelf resorted.
**Monthly:** fridge and pantry check against FIFO.
**A fixed day beats a reminder.** Reminders get dismissed.

question.text: Why does a fixed day beat a reminder?
options: A reminder can be dismissed; a habit runs by itself
question.explain: The point is to stop deciding.

cards.title: Why this is yours
cards.text: This is not about being helpful. It is about carrying weight.
points: **You generate washing, dishes and mess.**
**Somebody deals with it either way.**
**Doing your own share is not a favour.**
**Noticing without being asked** is the actual skill.

cards.title: Label the drawer
cards.text: Anyone who has lost a screw knows why.
points: **Sorted into labelled boxes**, not one tin.
**Labels are for your future self**, who has forgotten.
**Finding takes seconds** instead of minutes.
**Ten minutes of sorting** buys back hours.

cards.title: Reduce the friction, not your willpower
cards.text: Any system that needs effort every single time will be abandoned.
points: **A basket by the door** beats remembering to carry it up.
**One hook at the right height** beats a tidy pile.
**Design for the tired version of you.**
**That is who will be using it.**

question.text: A system that depends on remembering is a working system.
question.explain: It fails on the first tired evening. Design for the tired version of you.

cards.title: Designed for the tired version of you
cards.alt: Three wall hooks at child height with a bag and cap, a basket beneath and a key dish on a small shelf
cards.text: A hook at the right height beats remembering. That is the whole trick.

cards.title: A routine protects sleep
cards.text: The thing that actually makes you faster and stronger is the one a chaotic evening eats.
points: **Jobs done early** means bed at a fixed time.
**Fixed bedtime** is what makes training work.
**Eight to ten hours**, not six.
**Organisation is training**, indirectly.

cards.title: What to remember
points: One home for every object, where it is used.
Three loops: daily, weekly, monthly, on fixed days.
Design for the tired version of yourself.
Your own share is not a favour, and noticing is the skill.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 10 TLE, and the week that ties the term together: kitchen zoning, FIFO and clean-as-you-go are all the same principle, which is to make the decision once and then stop making it. The strongest card is the honest one (household work is his share of work he generates, not a favour) stated plainly and without moralising, with the real skill named as noticing without being asked. The gaming lens gives the week its most usable rule: design for the tired version of yourself, because that is who will be using the system. The growth lens closes the loop to training through sleep, which is true and is the argument he will actually accept.
discussion: Ask where one object's home should be, and why there.
Ask what belongs in the daily, weekly and monthly loops.
Ask what "design for the tired version of you" would change in his room.
Ask what work he generates in a week.
extension: Have him set up one real system (a hook, a basket, a labelled shelf) and run it for a week.
Have him write the three loops on a card and put it where he will see it.
misconceptions: "A reminder is a system." It can be dismissed.
"Tidying is about tidiness." It is about not deciding twice.
"Doing chores is helping out." It is carrying your own share.
